title: C Interview Craft and Classic Gotchas
relevance: Interviewers use classic C gotchas to test memory safety, undefined-behavior awareness, and whether candidates understand how foundational rules interact at their edges.

phases.goal: Establish the core C distinctions interviewers probe first: pointer operators, memory ownership, string storage, and static.

must_hit.point: *p++ (same as *(p++)) dereferences then advances the pointer; (*p)++ increments the pointed-to value because ++ binds tighter than *.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States both meanings and that post-increment binds more tightly than dereference.

must_hit.point: A dangling pointer points to freed or out-of-scope memory (using it is UB); a memory leak is allocated memory never freed after all pointers to it are lost.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates stale/invalid pointer from unreclaimable allocated memory until process death.

must_hit.point: char *s = "hello" points at a read-only string literal (typically .rodata); char s[] = "hello" copies into a mutable array that is safe to modify.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts read-only literal vs mutable copy and notes modifying the literal can segfault.

must_hit.point: static inside a function extends lifetime to the whole program while keeping local scope; at file scope it gives internal linkage to that translation unit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names both meanings: lifetime between calls, and linkage restricted to the current file.

probes: What is the difference between *p++, (*p)++, and *(p++)?
What is the difference between a dangling pointer and a memory leak?
What is the difference between char *s = "hello" and char s[] = "hello"?
What are the two distinct meanings of the static keyword?

hints.1: Think about what the operator applies to: the pointer or the value it points at.
hints.2: Separate operator precedence, storage duration/linkage, and where string data actually lives.
hints.3: *p++ advances p after yielding *p; (*p)++ changes *p; dangling vs leak is freed/out-of-scope vs never-freed; literal vs array is .rodata vs mutable copy; static is lifetime inside functions and internal linkage at file scope.

phases.goal: Show how declaration precedence, sizeof vs strlen, macros, padding, bits, and endianness actually evaluate.

must_hit.point: int *p[10] is an array of 10 pointers to int; int (*p)[10] is a pointer to an array of 10 ints because [] binds tighter than * unless parentheses force * first.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses spiral/precedence rule and does not treat pointer-to-array as int **.

must_hit.point: For char s[10] = "hi"; strlen(s) returns 2 (chars before null) while sizeof(s) is 10 (compile-time allocated array size).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives both results and warns sizeof on a decayed parameter yields pointer size, not array length.

must_hit.point: #define SQUARE(x) x * x is unsafe: SQUARE(1 + 2) expands to 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 evaluating to 5 not 9; SQUARE(i++) evaluates the argument twice and can cause UB; fix with ((x)*(x)) or prefer inline functions.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows textual expansion, the 5-not-9 case, double evaluation, and parenthesized or inline fix.

must_hit.point: sizeof(struct { char a; int b; }) can be 8 not 5 because the compiler inserts 3 padding bytes so int b is 4-byte aligned.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names padding/alignment and the serialization hazard of assuming packed layout.

must_hit.point: A non-zero unsigned integer is a power of two iff (x & (x - 1)) == 0 because a power of two has exactly one bit set.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the bitwise test and the one-bit-set rationale, not a divide-by-2 loop.

must_hit.point: Runtime endianness: set int num = 1, view as char *, and if *byte == 1 the machine is little-endian; endianness is byte layout, not bit-order.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes the byte-view test and distinguishes byte-order from bit-order.

probes: How do you read int *p[10] versus int (*p)[10]?
How do strlen(s) and sizeof(s) differ for char s[10] = "hi";?
What is the pitfall of #define SQUARE(x) x * x?
Why might sizeof(struct { char a; int b; }) be 8 instead of 5?
How do you test if a non-zero unsigned integer is a power of two?

hints.1: Ask what binds first and what is being measured: type layout, string length, or macro text.
hints.2: Walk declaration spiral, compile-time sizeof vs runtime strlen, macro expansion before evaluation, and alignment padding.
hints.3: Array-of-pointers vs pointer-to-array; strlen 2 / sizeof 10; SQUARE(1+2)→5; 3 pad bytes for 4-byte int alignment; (x&(x-1))==0; little-endian if low byte of 1 is 1.

phases.goal: Choose constants, interview pacing, and synchronization tools with the constraints the file spells out.

must_hit.point: Prefer const for typed/scoped non-modifiable values, #define for untyped preprocessor text with no scope, and enum for related named integer constants (better than #define for state machines); const int may not size a static array in C89 while #define or enum can.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Maps each tool to typed/scoped vs textual vs grouped integers and mentions the C89 array-size issue.

must_hit.point: C interview drive strategy: clarify constraints (e.g. 32-bit int, whether string.h is allowed), ship a simple safe baseline first, then refine to bitwise/pointer tricks, walk NULL/empty/max edges, and reject shortcuts that rely on signed overflow or strict-aliasing violations.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Orders clarify → brute force → optimize → edge cases → call out UB rather than jumping to clever code.

must_hit.point: Inline functions are vastly preferred over function-like macros for logic because macros are not function calls and mishandle precedence and multiple evaluation.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Rejects treating macros as functions and prefers inlines for logic.

probes: When should you use const vs #define vs enum for constants?
How should you approach writing C in an interview versus jumping straight to a clever solution?
Why prefer inline functions over macros for logic?

hints.1: Think about type, scope, and whether you need a working baseline before cleverness.
hints.2: Contrast typed constants, preprocessor text, and enums; then separate correctness pacing from micro-optimizations.
hints.3: const typed/scoped, #define textual/unscoped, enum for related ints (C89 array-size caveat); clarify→safe baseline→optimize→edges→name UB; prefer inline over macros.

phases.goal: Apply the rules under pressure: stack returns, volatile/ISR hazards, UB meaning, and classic output puzzles.

must_hit.point: Returning a pointer to a local is disastrous: the stack object is destroyed on return, so the caller holds an invalid address that the next call will overwrite; "sometimes works" is still always UB.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Ties stack lifetime to invalid returned address and rejects "it worked once" as defined.

must_hit.point: volatile forbids caching reads/writes when a value may change outside the current thread; required for memory-mapped registers and globals written by an ISR and read by the main loop; it does not give atomicity or stop CPU cache reordering, so it is not thread synchronization.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists the two required cases and explicitly denies using volatile to sync threads.

must_hit.point: Read-modify-write like x |= 0x01 is load/OR/store; an ISR between load and store can change x and be overwritten; x++ and bitwise ops are almost never atomic on a 32-bit MCU—disable interrupts briefly or use atomics.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains the three-step RMW race and the interrupt-disable or atomic fix.

must_hit.point: Do not call malloc or printf in an ISR: they are non-deterministic and lock-based; if the main loop held the lock, the ISR re-enter can deadlock.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Links ISR determinism to lock re-entry deadlock for stdio/allocation.

must_hit.point: Common UB includes NULL/uninitialized dereference, out-of-bounds access, and signed overflow; UB is not merely crash-or-wrap—the compiler may assume it never happens and optimize unpredictably.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names those three examples and the aggressive-assumption meaning of UB.

must_hit.point: Passing char str[] = "Antigravity" (12 chars) into char arr[] decays to a pointer, so sizeof(arr) prints pointer size (usually 8 on 64-bit, 4 on 32-bit), not 12.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States array-to-pointer decay and pointer-sized sizeof result.

must_hit.point: Mixing unsigned int a = 10 with int b = -20 promotes b to unsigned (e.g. 4294967276 on 32-bit), so a+b > 10 is true and prints Greater.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Cites usual arithmetic conversions and the Greater outcome.

must_hit.point: Writing a float via an unsigned int * violates strict aliasing (except char *); the compiler may ignore the write and still print 1.000000; do it safely with memcpy or a union in C99+.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names strict aliasing, possible stale 1.000000 print, and memcpy/union fix.

probes: Why is returning a pointer to a local variable disastrous?
What exactly does volatile do, and when is it required?
What is the read-modify-write atomicity hazard?
Why can't you call malloc or printf inside an ISR?
Name three common examples of Undefined Behavior.
What does the sizeof-on-decayed-array puzzle print, and why?

hints.1: Ask what still exists after return, what the compiler may cache, and what an ISR can interrupt.
hints.2: Connect stack lifetime, volatile vs atomics, RMW load/store windows, lock re-entry in ISRs, and conversion/aliasing rules in the puzzles.
hints.3: Locals die on return; volatile for MMIO/ISR shared state only; RMW is three steps; no malloc/printf in ISR; UB examples plus compiler freedom; decayed sizeof is pointer width; unsigned wins in a+b; float via int* is strict-aliasing UB.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: const gives a typed, scoped non-modifiable object (useful for parameters like const char *); #define is untyped textual substitution with no scope; enum groups related named integer constants with type and scope and is better than #define for state machines. In C89 a const int is not a constant expression for static array size, while #define or enum works.

tradeoffs.topic: brute-force baseline vs early bitwise/pointer cleverness
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Clarify sizes and library constraints, write the simple safe version first, then refine; only after a working baseline move to bitwise or pointer-arithmetic tricks, and explicitly reject shortcuts that depend on signed overflow or strict aliasing.
Macros ignore precedence and evaluate arguments multiple times (SQUARE(1+2)→5; SQUARE(i++) can be UB). Inline functions are vastly preferred for logic.

volatile only stops compiler elision of loads/stores for MMIO and ISR-shared globals; it does not guarantee atomicity or prevent CPU cache reordering, so it must not be used to synchronize threads—use proper atomics or locks instead.

gotchas.correction: *p++ / *(p++) yields the current *p then advances p; use (*p)++ to increment the value.

gotchas.trap: Treating a pointer to an array like int **
gotchas.correction: int (*p)[10] has different pointer-arithmetic scale than a double pointer; they are not interchangeable.

gotchas.trap: Believing free(p) sets p to NULL
gotchas.correction: free only returns memory to the allocator; p still holds the stale address unless you clear it yourself.

gotchas.trap: Thinking returning a pointer to a local "sometimes works" so it is okay
gotchas.correction: It is always undefined behavior even if the stack slot has not been overwritten yet.

gotchas.trap: Passing char *s = "hello" into a string-reversal that writes through s
gotchas.correction: The literal is read-only; modification can segfault—use a mutable char array copy.

gotchas.trap: Using sizeof on a function parameter declared char s[] expecting array or string length
gotchas.correction: The parameter has decayed to a pointer; sizeof yields pointer size, not the original array size.

gotchas.trap: Confusing static's scope with its lifetime or forgetting linkage
gotchas.correction: Inside a function static changes lifetime; at file scope it changes linkage to internal for that translation unit.

gotchas.trap: Using a const int as a static array size in C89
gotchas.correction: It is not a constant expression there; use #define or enum (or a newer standard that allows it).
They are textual; parenthesize aggressively or prefer inline functions to avoid precedence and double-evaluation bugs.

gotchas.trap: Detecting a power of two with a divide-by-2 loop only
gotchas.correction: Prefer (x & (x - 1)) == 0 for a non-zero unsigned value with exactly one bit set.
Endianness is about byte layout in memory, not bit order within a byte.

gotchas.trap: Assuming structs pack with no padding when serializing
gotchas.correction: Padding for alignment (e.g. 3 bytes after a char before an int) makes sizeof larger; do not blast raw structs to the network or a file.

gotchas.trap: Believing UB just means crash or wraparound
gotchas.correction: The compiler may assume UB never happens and optimize away checks, yielding unpredictable code.
It only inhibits compiler caching; it does not provide atomicity or stop CPU reordering.

gotchas.trap: Assuming x++ or bitwise updates are atomic on a 32-bit MCU
gotchas.correction: They are almost never atomic; protect with briefly disabled interrupts or atomic instructions.

gotchas.trap: Calling malloc or printf inside an ISR
gotchas.correction: They can lock and deadlock if the interrupted context already held the lock; keep ISRs fast and deterministic.

gotchas.trap: Modifying a variable twice without a sequence point (e.g. i = i++ + 1)
gotchas.correction: That is undefined behavior; the printed result is not predictable.
